subject: cyborgMedic
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: support-hero cyborg medic with a healing staff.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a full TypeScript module for a humanoid cyborg medic with a healing staff in an Overwatch-inspired style, aiming for a thorough but careful build given I can't test the SDK directly. I'm sketching the proportions first—roughly 1.85m tall with slightly heroic scaling.

I'm figuring out the color scheme and silhouette: white/blue armor with cyan-gold glow accents, a robotic arm and visor-style optic, plus a tall healing staff with a glowing emitter orb and caduceus-like ring, standing on a hex platform with a holo healing cross.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy—hips as root branching into spine, neck, head, and jaw, with shoulder-to-hand chains on each arm and hip-to-toe chains on each leg—and establishing the coordinate system with feet at y=0, figuring out exact joint heights for legs and arms using chain paths between named points.

I'm working through how chains with named joint lists map onto polyline or catmull paths—deciding to use straight polylines for limbs so corners can be smoothed during skinning, and working out how adding a toe joint after the ankle extends the leg chain with an extra tip joint, while considering whether to crop the sweep range to avoid an oddly thin boot segment between ankle and toe.

Now I'm settling on a simpler three-joint leg chain (hip, knee, ankle) where ankle becomes the chain's tip, adding the toe as a separate joint parented to that tip for the rigid foot geometry. For the sweep radius, I'm laying out keyed radius values along the leg's length—tapering from thigh to knee to ankle—roughly matching the proportional lengths of thigh and shin segments.

For the armor look, I'm planning layered plates over a base dark-suit sweep: thigh plates, knee pads, shin guards, and boots built from boxes and frustum shapes attached to bones, with positions and rotations defined in model-space coordinates.

I'll also set up a mirror helper to generate left/right variants by flipping the X sign, naming parts with L/R suffixes. For the character concept, I'm leaning toward an original cyborg medic design with teal/white armor and orange accents, featuring a robotic right arm, rather than a direct Mercy clone.

Fleshing out details: short swept hair with a ponytail, a glowing cyan mechanical eye, a tabard, and a healing staff in the left hand topped with a glowing crystal ring shaped like a cross. I'm also considering a backpack unit with a glowing cross symbol and small antenna fins for extra silhouette interest.

For the palette, I want a painterly soft look rather than hard cel-shaded toon style, so I'll build custom paint functions with gradients and subtle noise for the pale blue-white armor, keeping the color count mindful of atlas limits.

Now I'm planning out the SVG textures needed: a human eye and cyborg eye for the face, brows, mouth, chest emblem, backpack emblem, pauldron stripe, a forearm holo display with heartbeat, base rune ring, and staff glyph -- aiming for roughly 5-12 decal textures total.

I'm continuing to list these out: a medical cross emblem for chest/back, an ECG heartbeat screen for the forearm glow, a holo ring pattern for the base, a caduceus-style wrap for the staff, a chevron tabard pattern, a medkit label, floating "+" particle cards with glow, and a base floor tile pattern -- skipping a hair card since hair will use solid mass plus extruded blades instead.

Now I'm thinking through which emissive parts need the glow treatment -- cyber eye, visor, staff orb, chest light, arm lines, holo screen, and the plus-cards -- and planning the geometry build order. I want to keep the API usage safe and predictable since I can't test the code, favoring joints, chains, sweeps, extrudes, lathes, decals, cards, and lofts, while being careful with riskier calls like sticks. For face decals I'm considering placing a decal directly on the head's surface near the front, or alternatively using slightly offset textured planes in front of the face as a safer fallback.

For the head structure, I'm designing a stylized cranium as a squashed sphere with a separate hinged lower jaw piece underneath, plus a small face wedge for the nose and cheek area. The mouth will be built from small flattened pink-toned lip shapes split between the upper head and lower jaw, with a thin dark box as the mouth line between them, skipping teeth for simplicity. For facial features I'm planning decaled eyes with white sclera and iris, thin box eyebrows, a small nose shape, and a special cybernetic right eye done as a cyan decal with mechanical detailing around it.

Now I'm detailing that cybernetic eye plate as an extruded white-and-gold shape with a glowing line across the right cheek, plus mismatched ears -- a small human sphere ear on the left and a cylindrical cyber ear with a cyan ring and antenna on the right. For hair, I'm shaping a sleek swept-back cap using a partial sphere geometry with adjusted phi and theta ranges to cover the top and back of the head, then tilting it backward with an X-axis rotation so the hairline sits higher at the front.

I'm figuring out the rotation direction so the cap's rim rises properly at the forehead, then adding swept fringe blades across the forehead plus a ponytail built as a chained, tapered sweep of joints extending from the back of the head, using the "tail" role, topped off with a gold hair-tie band. For the torso, I'm considering a lofted body shape built from spine chain stations running from hips to chest.

Now I'm working out the spine chain joints from hips through spine1-3 up to the shoulders, then building the neck chain continuing from the top spine joint toward the head, making sure each chain's start position lines up with where the previous one ends.

I'm setting approximate body heights (hips ~0.95, shoulders ~1.46, neck base ~1.5, head center ~1.72, top of head ~1.84) and defining the head joint parented to the neck's top joint, figuring out its position and bone direction while reasoning that orientation won't matter much since I'm using model-space part placement.

Working out jaw placement...

I'm figuring out the loft cross-section dimensions — likely full width/height interpolated through station centers, with a default elliptical section using rx/ry rather than a box.

Now I'm planning the torso armor: a dark navy bodysuit with Overwatch-style white/gold/teal chest plating, a dangling tabard, abdomen plates, a pouch belt, hip tassets, and a backpack, starting with a tapered frustum box for the chest piece.

I'll add surface details to break up the plate look—a glowing cross emblem on the sternum, pauldrons shaped from partial hemispheres, a lathed collar ring, and a neck guard piece.

For the pauldrons I'm sculpting a half-dome shape tilted outward with a thin gold rim torus and teal accent stripe, positioned over each shoulder joint. Then I'm working out the arm chain geometry—shoulder, elbow, and rest pose points for a slightly separated limb stance.

For the rest pose I'll go with a loose A-pose, arms angled about 25° from the body with elbows bent slightly forward, and the left hand gripping a vertical staff that stands on the floor. I'm placing coordinates for the left shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand so the fist wraps naturally around the staff, then starting on the right arm's robotic proportions.

For the right arm, hanging naturally with an open hand, fingers pointing down and slightly splayed for rigging. For the fingers I'm chaining four digits plus a thumb on each hand, with the left curled partially around the staff to read as a grip while the right stays relaxed and open with fingers slightly fanned out.

Now I need to count the total joint budget to stay under the 160-joint limit: hips, spine, neck, head, and jaw give about 8 joints, legs add roughly 8 more, arms with clavicles add another 8, and then the fingers—each built from a base, mid, and tip—add significantly more per hand once I include the thumb chains.

Defining the hand frame and palm geometry...

Since the staff is vertical, I realize the four fingers should stack vertically along the pole, each one wrapping horizontally around it as a C-shaped arc at increasing heights—I'm working out the geometry for how each finger curls from the body side around the front of the staff back toward the palm.

Working out the rotation direction around the Y axis to sweep the fingers from the back-inner side across the front of the staff, so the arc starts near -X and sweeps roughly 200° toward the front.

For the finger joints, I'll use a chain with `count: 3` to reduce each arc into three resampled joints, naming them with a base like "fingerIndexL1..3" to keep them unique, parented to the wrist tip joint.

I'm sweeping the fingers with a glove color and tapered radii, starting inside the palm. The thumb for the left hand gets a rough polyline path wrapping over the top of the hand with a 2-joint chain, and now I'm sketching the right hand's open, relaxed pose for the cyborg arm.

Positioning right hand fingers...

Figuring out finger positions with palm facing inward, thumb pointing forward-down, then planning a helper function to build each finger as a chain of joints from sampled points so I can reuse it for both hands.

I'll just compute the arc positions directly with trig instead, using an angle φ around Y from +Z toward +X to place each finger base, sweeping roughly 200° so fingers start on the inner-back side and end on the outer side, with the palm occupying the remaining inner/back arc.

I'm now placing the palm box at roughly φ=-150°, giving a center near (0.40, 0.865, 0.103) relative to the wrist, with the staff centered around (0.42, y, 0.14) and the palm sized about 0.045×0.085×0.06, checking that this keeps the fingers wrapping correctly around the staff radius.

Next I'm stacking the four fingers vertically within the palm, spacing them evenly around y≈0.83–0.90 with roughly 0.021 diameter each, then positioning the thumb from its base near the palm's top-inner edge extending outward and upward along the staff.

For the staff itself, I'm placing it vertically around x=0.42, z=0.14, with the pole running from near the floor (y≈0.01) up past the character's height to around y=1.95.

Designing the staff head now: dark shaft with gold bands and wrapped grip, a spike foot at bottom, and a crescent-shaped crown up top holding a glowing orb with a cross inside, plus a small rotating ring and wings around it. Writing the geometry for the shaft cylinder, gold collar, and crescent arm sweeps...

The orb glows teal, with a tilted glowing torus ring and crossing white boxes inside for the cross, plus a top finial spike and gold feather-like wings near the collar. I'm defining crescent prong paths using curved sweeps and placing the orb above the collar, then deciding the staff should be rigged to follow the left wrist joint so it moves naturally with the character's hand.

Now I'm setting up the arm chain: a clavicle joint parented to the spine, then shoulder-elbow-wrist joints forming the arm path, each assigned the "arm" role with varying sweep radii for the upper arm.

I want asymmetric arms for the Overwatch cyborg look: the left arm organic under a navy suit sleeve with a forearm bracer and gloved hand, while the right arm is robotic with thinner gunmetal segments, exposed piston details, and white shell armor plates built from frustum boxes.

For the robotic arm's cyan glow, I'm placing torus rings along the forearm axis to simulate energy bands, and using thin rods across the elbow joint to represent pistons, with limb direction and lerp helpers to position everything correctly in model space.

Now I'm mapping out leg joint positions—hip, knee, ankle, toe—for both sides, considering a partially mechanical right leg with an exposed shin and spring coil detail pulled from the clockwork kit.

I'll import the glow and clockwork kits (specifically metal, coil, and panelled helpers) to give the cyborg limb its mechanical look, keeping kit usage minimal and safe rather than reaching for extras like gear trains.

Now I'm designing the armor paint function, blending a cool white base with directional shading toward the top, adding scuff noise for texture, and darkening grime near the feet where the model touches ground.

For the suit I want a navy base with a vertical gradient and subtle seam lines for a tech feel, keeping the shading simple with countershading. Gold trim will use the metal paint helper with a gilt finish for the Overwatch-style accents, teal stays flat, and skin uses a warm tan countershade with blush highlights on the cheeks.

For hair I'm settling on a deep brown base with a warm orange highlight streak that fades by vertical position rather than something more exotic like plum or teal-black.

Now I'm thinking through the base platform geometry — a hexagonal cylinder around 0.72 radius, positioned to account for the staff extending the character's footprint, and making sure the lowest points of the model actually touch the floor plane.

Rather than hand-calculating offsets everywhere, I decide to define the character in simple feet-at-zero coordinates and write a small helper that shifts every point upward by the platform's ground height, so the whole figure sits correctly on top of the base without me tracking the offset manually at each vertex.

Designing the hex platform geometry...

For props, I'm adding a medkit case near the front-left with a cross decal, plus a small hovering medical drone with a sphere body, ring, and eye. Since scenery without an explicit bone attaches to the nearest joint by default, I need to assign these props explicit bone anchors rather than letting them snap to whatever leg bone is closest.

I'm resolving the rig hierarchy: deciding whether to name the root joint "root" with "hips" as its spine child, or make "hips" itself the root joint, since the convention treats hips/pelvis as either the root or the first spine joint -- and I'll anchor the scenery props to whichever joint stays fixed rather than moving with locomotion.

Now I'm planning the medic's backpack details on the spine3 bone: a paneled box shape with glowing cross emblem, exhaust nozzles, and two angled wing-like plates for a caduceus-inspired silhouette.

Working out the wing outline curve...

I'll set the wing outline direction so it extends outward and backward from the body, mounted near the backpack, with three fanned feather layers of decreasing size in white, teal, and gold, each rotated slightly to create a spread effect.

For the chest, I'm thinking of adding a medic emblem as a small decal plane positioned just in front of the chest plate surface, tilted slightly to match its angle.

I'll shape the chest plate as a cuirass wrapping the whole torso, slightly larger than the suit beneath so it fully encloses front, sides, and back where the backpack attaches, with an octagonal ellipse cross-section at each station. The suit will peek out at the waist and arms, keeping that blocky puppet-armor look with a white cuirass and teal accent band.

For the torso loft itself, I'm defining stations from the hip up to the upper chest with widths and heights narrowing then widening slightly, tied to the hips and spine bones -- though I need to check whether the hip joint placement at the lowest station actually aligns with where the legs parent in, since the bone weighting there matters for how the loft deforms.

For the belt I'm weighing options between a lathe ring versus scaling a mesh non-uniformly to match the elliptical hip profile, since lathe shapes are inherently circular and I'd need to squash it to fit the 0.32×0.2 width-to-height ratio by adjusting the mesh's scale directly rather than through the part options.

I'm reasoning through how scale applies relative to the mesh's rotation — since the geometry gets scaled in its own local axes before any rotation is applied, using a `scale: [1,1,0.65]` option on the part should correctly squash the belt along the model's geometry axes regardless of the bone's orientation.

For lathe or extrude shapes the scale option isn't available, so I'd need to apply it via `part.scale.set` instead, though the geometry frame there is less certain since the shape may already be baked relative to its placement. To stay safe I'll just use a cylinder or torus geometry scaled on one axis to get the elliptical belt shape, using a closed cylinder so it reads as a solid disc wrapping the torso rather than an open tube.

Now I'm planning out the actual part list by section. For the head I'm sketching roughly 25 pieces — skull, jaw, cheeks, nose, brows, eye decals, ears, a cyber ear plate, hair cap, fringe blades, a ponytail with ties and blades, lips, chin, neck sweep and collar, plus a cybernetic eye plate with a glowing ring around one eye. For the torso I'm starting with a lofted suit base and a chest cuirass.

For the rest of the body I'm laying out the torso parts: chest emblem, collar ring, teal band, abdomen plates, belt with a hex buckle, side pouches, and a hanging cloth tabard. Since extrusion doesn't support textures, I'm switching to double-sided textured cards for the tabard, hanging it from the belt with a slight lean and gentle forward bend so it flares outward naturally.

I'm now planning the backpack, wings, and glowing cross for the back, along with mismatched pauldrons (bulky white left shoulder, smaller cyborg metal right shoulder), trim rings, and shoulder lights. For the legs I'm sketching thigh plating, knee pads, shin guards, and boots, but making the right leg mechanical with a metal shin, coil spring, piston, and ankle servo instead of a normal suit sleeve.

With roughly 250 parts total achievable through helper functions and mirrored loops, I'm moving on to double-checking the API calls, starting with the builder creation and whether a larger paint size is needed for finer details.

Writing joint and chain hierarchy code...

Recalculating the skeleton coordinates: shoulders at 1.44, neck base at 1.5, with the neck curving forward through 1.57 to 1.66, and the skull center placed around y=1.76 with a slight forward z offset.

Checking total height with skull radius and hair added gets close to 1.9, which feels heroic rather than strictly realistic, but I decide that's acceptable for this character scale. I'm tweaking hip height and torso proportions slightly to keep the total around 1.91, then locking in the skull center position for the head joint definition.

Now I'm figuring out neck and skull placement precisely, setting the neck path curve toward the head joint and sizing the skull sphere so the top of the head lands near 1.885 and the jawline near 1.65, giving an overall height close to 1.91 with hair included.

I'm computing where the eyes sit on the face relative to the skull sphere's curvature, working out the front surface depth at the eye x-position so the decal placement lines up correctly with the sphere's geometry.

Now I'm shaping the jaw as a separate lower hemisphere attached beneath the cranium sphere, checking how its radius compares to the cranium's cross-section at the same height so the two pieces blend without an awkward seam.

I'm calculating the theta cutoff angle for the cranium sphere so its open bottom stays hidden, then checking where the mouth line falls on the jaw around y≈1.70.

For lips, I'm placing small flattened spheroids directly on the head geometry: an upper lip positioned at the cranium's cut edge near (0, 1.728, 0.152), and a lower lip on the jaw bone near (0, 1.705, 0.15), working out the local surface radius and front z-offset at each height.

Rather than compute the exact surface coordinates algebraically, I'll switch to a ray-casting approach — shooting a ray from in front of the head straight back to find where it hits the surface, then attaching parts there, since that's more robust than manual geometry math.

Attaching code for lips...

Combining skull and jaw into one surface so raycasts find the outermost hit works well for placing eye decals too. I'll call decal with the surface, hit point, and direction to mirror for the left and right sides.

Since the drawing is naturally the creature's right eye as drawn, I'll mirror it for the left eye using the toon kit's mirror convention. The right eye should get a separate cyber-texture decal with a surrounding plate, while the left stays organic.

I also need to guard against null ray hits in case the surface query fails, so I'll assert non-null on the ray cast.

Checking the surface query on built parts to confirm triangles are evaluated in world space, which seems fine. For the cranium I'm using a partial sphere geometry scaled onto the head bone with a flat skin material, and I'm not worried about paint coordinates since they're model-space regardless of scale.

For the ears, I'm placing a small scaled sphere for the organic left ear and a cylinder-with-ring for the cyber right ear. Now I'm working out the nose geometry...

Actually, I'm reconsidering the nose placement — using a stick anchored to a surface hit point so the cone naturally orients along the surface normal, pointing outward correctly. For the brows, I'm testing whether placing flat boxes at fixed offsets floats off the face surface, so I'm switching to sticking them to hits with a spin rotation to align with the brow angle instead.

For the left brow with positive rotation, the outer end lifts, giving more of an arched or mildly surprised look rather than angry.

Working out the rotation math confirms rotation = s*5° gives the correct outer-up tilt for each eyebrow side. I'm now positioning the brow piece slightly off the surface using the hit point plus a small offset along the surface normal.

For the brow shape itself, since the surface curves outward ~25° near the edges but the brow is nearly flat, I'm checking whether a thicker box (0.014 instead of 0.012) avoids visible gaps at the ends, or whether I should just let it ride along the normal direction with no extra spin to keep things simple.

Instead I'm considering rotating the brow's box geometry around its normal axis (Y) to slant it within the surface plane, relying on the known convention that on front-facing hits x points toward the model's right and z runs upward along the surface.

Working through the rotation math, I figure out for each brow which end is the "outer" end based on its x-sign, so I can determine the sign of the rotation angle φ needed to raise or lower that outer corner — negative φ for the right brow and the opposite relationship for the left brow, since they're mirrored across the model's x-axis.

I'm not going to overthink the tiny ambiguity in direction here since the hit normals at the brow area don't have huge x components anyway. Now shifting to the eye decals, I'm planning to size the eye texture around 60×40 pixels for a wider, semi-realistic Overwatch-style look.

Writing eye and leg positioning code...

I'm checking that the chain's first joint aligns with the hip parent location, then setting up a sweep over the leg chain with a tapering radius profile from thigh to ankle across several keys along the path.

For the right leg, I plan to split the sweep into two segments at the knee—thigh portion suited, shin portion mechanical—using different materials on each half so the two sections join smoothly at a shared knee ring.

I'll write a generic piecewise-linear interpolation helper to define the leg's radius profile from a table of control points, which handles the rounded cap transition at the knee cleanly. Then for leg armor, I'm placing angled frustum boxes along the thigh offset slightly forward for the plate shape.

For orientation consistency, I'm establishing a rule: since bones pointing down have their forward direction naturally mapping to +Z, I'll always sweep frustumBox segments from top to bottom so the normal stays forward rather than flipping backward. The thigh plate will use width along x and a thin front-back thickness along z, matching this top-to-bottom convention.

Placing the plate center offset forward from the thigh's circular cross-section, interpolated along the hip-to-knee line based on thigh radius. Now I'm defining the knee pad as a flattened hexagonal cylinder oriented to face forward.

Still building leg geometry...

I'm splitting the sole into heel and ball sections with specific box dimensions, then shaping the boot upper with a shaft, instep box, and toe cap sphere, with heel/sole in dark tones, upper in white with a teal stripe, and the toe cap in gold.

Now I'm planning chunky Overwatch-style boot plates and thinking through the overall code structure, aiming for a compact but comprehensive implementation while watching for TypeScript strictness issues like unused parameters. I'm setting up imports from the builder library and its kits for geometry, shading, and effects utilities.

Still writing imports...

I need to make sure every imported type and utility actually gets used to satisfy strict unused-locals checks, then I'm defining the builder instance and some small helper constants and vector functions for positioning joints with a slight ground offset.

Writing part and box helpers...

Now I'm sketching the SVG for an almond-shaped human eye with a white base.

Still writing SVG code...

I'm verifying the lash flick coordinates stay within the viewBox and confirming the iris gets clipped properly by the almond shape, then starting on a cyber-styled eye variant with a dark circular base.

Writing more SVG rings...

Then I consider whether glow effects work on textured decal parts, confirming they apply based on the texture's own colors so the dark ring portion stays dark due to low emissive values.

Now I'm designing a hexagonal badge emblem with a cross symbol, layering outer and inner borders in teal and gold tones with a bright cross shape in the center.

For the forearm display, I'm planning a dark panel with a cyan ECG waveform instead of relying on text rendering, keeping it simple with lines only. And for the floor holo-ring, I'm laying out concentric circles, dashed rings, hex ticks, and a central cross pattern with a transparent center so the base shows through.

Now I'm designing the tabard as a pointed-bottom shield shape with an ivory-teal gradient, gold edge stroke, central teal band, and small cross emblem, sized to hang from the belt over the thigh. I'm also adding a glowing teal plus-shaped particle effect, scattering card-like frames in a spiral around the staff orb.

For orienting these card frames, I'm working out how each should stand upright facing the flow direction, with its bottom edge anchored to the frame point and its center offset upward by half its length so it reads correctly when viewed from downstream.

I'm also setting `cross: true` so the cards are visible from any angle, sizing them around .06, and confirming the glow helper can accept the mesh array that cards returns. For bone attachment, I'm pinning the cards explicitly to the staff joint rather than letting them auto-select the nearest joint, since that could risk grabbing the wrong bone near the orb.

For the medkit, I'll reuse a simple cross texture rather than the full emblem. I'm planning a textured plane on the outer forearm for a screen effect with glow, skipping any hair texture in favor of paint, and considering whether a small back flap or cape card is worth adding beyond the tabard. I'm tallying up the texture set so far — eye, cyber, emblem, ECG, holo, tabard, plus-cross, kit label — around eight textures, and weighing whether to add a shoulder stripe/badge texture too.

Deciding to skip tiny shoulder chevron drawings and keep the texture count around 8-9. I'm settling on roughly ten paint materials covering armor, suit, skin, hair, gilt metal, blued steel, rubber, and tiled iron panels, plus a flat color palette of teal, navy, cream, red, and a warm orange accent to match an Overwatch-style look, keeping colors under the 64 limit with a teal glow set.

Starting the actual build now, setting up the module metadata and the initial builder function for the cyborg medic model.

Writing paint functions...

Writing hair gradient code...

I'll use polished steel for the cyborg arm shell, combined with white plates and a cyan glow. Now I'm working out the skeleton joint positions for both arms symmetrically, setting shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates with mirrored offsets for left and right sides.

I'm placing the hand palm positions relative to each wrist, then setting up the clavicle joints parented to the spine, debating whether to assign a role like "arm" or leave it unspecified since the chain role matters more than the individual joint's role.

Now I'm defining the arm chain itself with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the clavicle, verifying the shoulder joint aligns with the clavicle's endpoint. I'm checking the x-coordinates to confirm the side convention, then computing segment lengths—roughly 0.29 for the upper arm and 0.26 for the forearm—to figure out where the elbow falls along a full-length sweep, planning to color the whole arm sweep with the suit material.

I'm designing the right arm as the cyborg/robotic side: a suited sleeve with tapering radius from shoulder to elbow, then switching to a steel-colored armored sweep for the forearm, with a gunmetal ball joint at the elbow and chunky frustum-box plating for the gauntlet.

For the staff joint, I'm attaching it to the wrist tip of the left arm chain, then setting up a helper so armor plates can attach to either the shoulder or elbow joint depending on whether they're on the upper arm or forearm. Now I'm moving on to the torso.

I'll skip the sides parameter and use the default instead. For the chest cuirass loft, I'm using the ARMOR color with the spine bone chain, checking that the stations align properly along the spine path, then working out the specific station positions with their widths and heights for the cuirass shape.

Comparing the torso suit stations, which are narrower at waist and chest than the cuirass that will cover them, fits the hero-style wide shoulders and narrow waist silhouette. Now I'm figuring out the abdomen plates beneath the cuirass -- three stacked, ribbed horizontal cylinder segments alternating between ARMOR and teal colors, sized to peek out from under the suit.

Now I'm adding a belt with a gold buckle gem at the front, then working out hip armor plates using scaled spheres on either side of the pelvis.

For the tabard and back tail cloth, I'm setting up card frames hanging from the belt front with a lean and bend so they curl forward toward the flow direction at the tip, flaring outward as they drape down.

Since the card faces the flow direction, when viewed from downstream it displays the drawing upside down with the root edge at the top rather than mirrored — so I'll need to draw the actual tabard artwork inverted, with the free end appearing at the top of my design and the root attachment edge at the bottom, to compensate for this orientation flip.

Still drawing the shield outline... The problem states "upside down, not mirrored" — meaning it's a vertical flip, not a 180° rotation, so the u-axis stays unchanged with u pointing to the viewer's right while v flips.

Since the cross is horizontally symmetric, I can just design the tabard in its final world orientation (belt at top, point at bottom) and then apply a vertical flip transform to the whole SVG to get the correct downstream view.

For the backpack, I'm placing a box near the character's upper back with a cross glow plate as a textured plane on its rear face, oriented to face backward so the emblem is visible, with emitters positioned at the sides.

Now I'm working out the pauldrons — modeling the left one as a dome-shaped hemisphere positioned at the shoulder joint, and figuring out the rotation so the dome tilts outward away from the body.

I'm working through the Euler rotation order issue for the torus to lie flat and tilt correctly, considering whether to use the `dir`/`axis` approach instead since the rotation composition order is ambiguous.

I decide to rely on `dir`/`axis` for most shapes (dome, cylinder, cone) rather than raw rotation, reserving rotation only for simple box cases. For the shoulder pauldrons, I'm layering a dome, gold rim torus, teal stripe torus, and glowing shoulder lamp sphere, then starting to plan the collar/neck sweep.

Now I'm detailing the neck chain sweep with caps, the collar ring cylinder, and head/hair elements, then thinking through cyber-details like a half-face plate and a thin torus ring around the right eye for a tech accent.

Fitting the eye rim plate...

Still adding small cyber armor details...

Now I'm plotting the ponytail as a catmull chain curving back and down from the crown toward the upper back, checking its endpoint doesn't collide with the backpack's depth and height range.

Adding hair strand sweeps...

Actually, simpler to use flattened scaled spheres for the fringe instead of a swept outline — three tilted ellipsoids hugging the forehead, computing their placement so they sit flush against the head's curved surface near the hairline.

I'm trying to figure out where the hair cap's front edge should sit relative to the hairline and brow, working through the sphere geometry and tilt angle to get the fringe positioned naturally above the forehead rather than too low.

Using a direction vector instead of raw rotation angles for the pole makes it clearer to tilt toward -z, so I'll specify the pole as pointing mostly up and slightly backward, keeping the ellipsoid scale defined in the geometry's own tilted axes.

I'm settling on hair radii around 7% larger than the skull's in each dimension, since the shape is nearly spherical the tilt shouldn't cause noticeable poking through at the front-top, though I should double check that region stays clear.

Checking the remaining margins confirms the fit works, with the front edge tight but acceptable since the fringe covers it. Now I'm planning additional hair details—side-swept locks, gold hair clips, and a fringe made of blade-like extrudes sweeping to one side—and sketching the outline coordinates for one of these curved locks.

Mapping blade outline coordinates...

I want the hair swept asymmetrically to one side—more blades toward model-left, with a smaller counter-sweep on the right for balance. Now I'm sketching the jaw joint placement for the face rig.

Still shaping facial geometry...

Checking the mouth region alignment, I find the front surfaces of the jaw hemisphere and cranium meet continuously at the join point. I'll place the upper lip near y≈1.739 on the cranium side and the lower lip around 1.708 on the jaw side to keep the mouth looking natural across the seam.
